{{short description|Operation that combines groups}}
{{for|a free product of rings and algebras|free product of associative algebras}}
{{Group theory sidebar|Basics}}

In [[mathematics]], specifically [[group theory]], the '''free product''' is an operation that takes two [[group (mathematics)|groups]] {{tmath|G}} and {{tmath|H}} and constructs a new group {{tmath|G * H}}. The result contains both {{tmath|G}} and {{tmath|H}} as [[subgroup]]s, is [[Generating set of a group|generated]] by the elements of these subgroups, and is the “[[universal property|universal]]” group having these properties, in the sense that any two homomorphisms from {{tmath|G}} and {{tmath|H}} into a group {{tmath|K}} factor uniquely through a homomorphism from {{tmath|G * H}} to {{tmath|K}}. Unless one of the groups {{tmath|G}} and {{tmath|H}} is trivial, the free product is always infinite. The construction of a free product is similar in spirit to the construction of a [[free group]] (the universal group with a given set of generators).

The free product is the [[coproduct]] in the [[category of groups]]. That is, the free product plays the same role in group theory that [[disjoint union]] plays in [[set theory]], or that the [[direct sum of modules|direct sum]] plays in [[module theory]]. Even if the groups are commutative, their free product is not, unless one of the two groups is the [[trivial group]]. Therefore, the free product is not the coproduct in the [[category of abelian groups]].

The free product is important in [[algebraic topology]] because of [[van Kampen's theorem]], which states that the [[fundamental group]] of the [[union (set theory)|union]] of two [[Connected space|path-connected]] [[topological space]]s whose intersection is also path-connected is always an '''amalgamated free product''' of the fundamental groups of the spaces.  In particular, the fundamental group of the [[wedge sum]] of two spaces (i.e. the space obtained by joining two spaces together at a single point) is, under certain conditions given in the Seifert van-Kampen theorem, the free product of the fundamental groups of the spaces.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hatcher |first=Allen |date=2001 |title=Algebraic Topology |url=https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/AT/AT.pdf |url-status=live |website=Cornell Math}}</ref>

Free products are also important in [[Bass–Serre theory]], the study of groups [[Group action (mathematics)|acting]] by automorphisms on [[Tree (graph theory)|trees]].  Specifically, any group acting with finite vertex stabilizers on a tree may be constructed from [[finite group]]s using amalgamated free products and [[HNN extension]]s.  Using the action of the [[modular group]] on a certain [[tessellation]] of the [[hyperbolic geometry|hyperbolic plane]], it follows from this theory that the modular group is [[isomorphic]] to the free product of [[cyclic group]]s of orders 4 and 6 amalgamated over a cyclic group of order 2.

== Construction ==
If {{tmath|G}} and {{tmath|H}} are groups, a ''[[word (group theory)|word]]'' on {{tmath|G}} and {{tmath|H}} is a [[sequence]] of the form <math>s_1 s_2 \cdots s_n</math>, where each {{tmath|s_i}} is either an element of {{tmath|G}} or an element of {{tmath|H}}. Such a word may be ''reduced'' using the following operations:
* remove an instance of the identity element (of either {{tmath|G}} or {{tmath|H}}), or
* replace a pair {{tmath|g_1g_2}} by its product in {{tmath|G}}, or a pair {{tmath|h_1h_2}} by its product in {{tmath|H}}.
Every reduced word is either the empty sequence, contains exactly one element of {{tmath|G}} or {{tmath|H}}, or is an alternating sequence of elements of {{tmath|G}} and elements of {{tmath|H}}, e.g.
: <math>g_1 h_1 g_2 h_2 \cdots g_k h_k.</math>
The '''free product''' {{tmath|G * H}} is the group whose elements are the reduced words in {{tmath|G}} and {{tmath|H}}, under the operation of concatenation followed by reduction.

For example, if {{tmath|G}} is the infinite cyclic group <math>\langle x\rangle</math>, and {{tmath|H}} is the infinite cyclic group <math>\langle y\rangle</math>, then every element of {{tmath|G * H}} is an alternating product of powers of {{tmath|x}} with powers of {{tmath|y}}.  In this case, {{tmath|G * H}} is isomorphic to the free group generated by {{tmath|x}} and {{tmath|y}}.

== Presentation ==
Suppose that
: <math>G = \langle S_G \mid R_G \rangle</math>
is a [[Presentation of a group|presentation]] for ''G'' (where ''S''<sub>''G''</sub> is a set of generators and ''R''<sub>''G''</sub> is a set of relations), and suppose that
: <math>H = \langle S_H \mid R_H \rangle</math>
is a presentation for ''H''.  Then
: <math>G * H = \langle S_G \cup S_H \mid R_G \cup R_H \rangle.</math> 
That is, ''G'' ∗ ''H'' is generated by the generators for ''G'' together with the generators for ''H'', with relations consisting of the relations from ''G'' together with the relations from ''H'' (assume here no notational clashes so that these are in fact [[disjoint union]]s).

=== Examples ===
For example, suppose that ''G'' is a cyclic group of order 4,
: <math>G = \langle x \mid x^4 = 1 \rangle,</math>
and ''H'' is a cyclic group of order 5
: <math>H = \langle y \mid y^5 = 1 \rangle.</math>
Then ''G'' ∗ ''H'' is the infinite group
: <math>G * H = \langle x, y \mid x^4 = y^5 = 1 \rangle.</math>

Because there are no relations in a free group, the free product of free groups is always a free group.  In particular,
: <math>F_m * F_n \cong F_{m+n},</math>
where ''F''<sub>''n''</sub> denotes the free group on ''n'' generators.

Another example is the [[modular group]] <math>PSL_2(\mathbf Z)</math>. It is isomorphic to the free product of two cyclic groups:<ref>{{cite journal | first = Roger C. | last=  Alperin |authorlink=Roger C. Alperin| title = PSL<sub>2</sub>(Z) = Z<sub>2</sub> * Z<sub>3</sub> | journal = Amer. Math. Monthly | volume = 100 | pages = 385–386 | date = April 1993 | doi = 10.1080/00029890.1993.11990418 }}</ref> 
: <math>PSL_2(\mathbf Z) \cong (\mathbf Z / 2 \mathbf Z) \ast (\mathbf Z / 3 \mathbf Z).</math>

== Generalization: Free product with amalgamation ==
The more general construction of '''free product with amalgamation''' is correspondingly a special kind of [[pushout (category theory)|pushout]] in the same [[category theory|category]]. Suppose <math>G</math> and <math>H</math> are given as before, along with monomorphisms (i.e. injective [[group homomorphisms]]):
: <math>\varphi : F \rightarrow G \ \, </math> and <math>\ \, \psi : F \rightarrow H,</math>
where <math>F</math> is some arbitrary group. Start with the free product <math>G * H</math> and adjoin as relations
: <math>\varphi(f)\psi(f)^{-1}=1</math>
for every <math>f</math> in <math>F</math>. In other words, take the [[Conjugate closure|smallest normal subgroup]] <math>N</math> of <math>G * H</math> containing all elements on the [[Left-hand side and right-hand side of an equation|left-hand side]] of the above equation, which are tacitly being considered in <math>G * H</math> by means of the inclusions of <math>G</math> and <math>H</math> in their free product. The free product with amalgamation of <math>G</math> and <math>H</math>, with respect to <math>\varphi</math> and <math>\psi</math>, is the [[quotient group]]
: <math>(G * H)/N.\,</math>

The amalgamation has forced an identification between <math> \varphi(F) </math> in <math>G</math> with <math>\psi(F)</math> in <math>H</math>, element by element. This is the construction needed to compute the fundamental group of two connected spaces joined along a path-connected subspace, with <math>F</math> taking the role of the fundamental group of the subspace. See: [[Seifert–van Kampen theorem]]. 

Karrass and [[Donald Solitar|Solitar]] have given a description of the subgroups of a free product with amalgamation.<ref>A. Karrass and D. Solitar (1970) [https://www.ams.org/journals/tran/1970-150-01/S0002-9947-1970-0260879-9/S0002-9947-1970-0260879-9.pdf The subgroups of a free product of two groups with an amalgamated subgroup], [[Transactions of the American Mathematical Society]] 150: 227–255.</ref> For example, the homomorphisms from <math>G</math> and <math>H</math> to the quotient group <math>(G * H)/N</math> that are induced by <math>\varphi</math> and <math>\psi</math> are both injective, as is the induced homomorphism from <math>F</math>.

Free products with amalgamation and a closely related notion of [[HNN extension]] are basic building blocks in Bass–Serre theory of groups acting on trees.

== In other branches ==
One may similarly define free products of other algebraic structures than groups, including [[algebra over a field|algebras over a field]].  Free products of algebras of [[random variable]]s play the same role in defining "[[free independence|freeness]]" in the theory of [[free probability]] that [[Cartesian product]]s play in defining [[statistical independence]] in classical [[probability theory]].
